questions.q: Per this lesson, what single question determines a catalog's entire value?
options: When someone searches, do they find the right answer quickly?
How many total tables does the catalog contain?
How much did the catalog software cost to license?
How visually attractive is the catalog's user interface?
questions.explain: Perfect metadata that nobody can find is worthless — search quality is the one capability everything else is secondary to.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four catalog capabilities named in this lesson?
options: Full-text search across business and technical metadata
Faceted filtering by owner, system, or status
Relationship navigation between glossary and dictionary
Automatic deletion of any table older than one year
questions.explain: The four capabilities are full-text search, faceted filtering, relationship navigation, and usage-based ranking — automatic deletion isn't a catalog search capability.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say faceted search depends specifically on the work done in Chapters 2 through 4?
options: Because filtering by owner, status, and sensitivity requires the consistent, structured metadata fields those chapters taught how to document
Because Chapters 2 through 4 are unrelated to search functionality entirely
Because faceted search only works on databases with fewer than ten tables
Because Chapter 4's content is required by law to appear in every catalog
questions.explain: A general web search lacks reliable structured fields to filter on; a data catalog has them because of the consistent documentation standards from earlier chapters.

questions.q: In the worked 'customer revenue' search example, why does OrderTotal rank above a table nobody queries, even if both mention 'customer'?
options: Usage-based ranking surfaces results that are actually queried in production above ones that aren't
OrderTotal's column name has more letters
Tables are always ranked alphabetically regardless of usage
The unused table was deleted automatically
questions.explain: Usage information from Lesson 20 lets the catalog prioritize actively-relied-upon results over technically-matching but ignored ones.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what happens when a catalog returns an unsorted list of every table containing a search keyword?
options: It forces the user to read through dozens of irrelevant results — exactly what a poorly built catalog does
This is considered the ideal, gold-standard search behavior
It is impossible for any catalog software to produce this result
It automatically converts into a faceted search after one use
questions.explain: The lesson contrasts this poor outcome directly against the good, ranked result set in the worked example — flat unsorted results are barely more useful than no search at all.
